newsitem.title: CHINA: First shipment of Chinese fruit on its way to U.S.
newsitem.headline: First shipment of Chinese fruit on its way to U.S.

text.p: Two containers of lychees, said to be the first Chinese fruit ever to be exported to the United States, are on the way to California, signalling a major breakthrough in bilateral food trade, U.S. officials said on Tuesday.

The shipment had been made possible with the certification this week of Chinese inspectors who could ensure the fruit reached U.S. standards, said Ray Miyamoto, area director of the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) in Beijing.

The exotic lychees -- sweet, pitted, white-fleshed fruit encased in a red leathery skin -- were trucked from southern Guangdong province to Hong Kong, from where they were shipped to the U.S. West Coast and should arrive in two weeks, he said.
"This opens the gate for any fruit that requires cold treatment to be exported from China to the United States," he said.
Another U.S. official said the shipment was a huge step forward in the often-troubled agricultural trade relationship between Beijing and Washington.
"Trade is trade, and this signals tremendous progress in the agricultural relationship between the two countries," he said on condition of anonymity.
Under regulations approved last August, APHIS personnel certified the Chinese inspectors to initiate cold treatment, a process that ensures the fruit is free of fruit fly, Miyamoto told Reuters.
The process was then continued in transit, he said.
Chinese inspectors had also been certified to initiate cold treament on Chinese "ya" pears from certain groves in northern Hebei province, he said.
Cold transit also included the use of ice water to maintain high humidity on the container ship to prevent the fruit drying out before reaching the United States, Miyamoto said.
The only U.S. region that grew lychees was Florida, though some small quantities were imported from Taiwan, he said. They were regarded as an exotic fruit in the United States.
Fruit has long been a contentious issue between Beijing and Washington, and the subject of exhaustive negotiations on phytosanitary, or plant health, issues.
A number of protocols have been signed in recent years, most pertaining to Beijing's application to join the international free trade club, the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
Last month, the first official shipment of U.S. cherries arrived in China -- subject to 48 percent import duty plus a value-added tax -- under agreements reached in a 1995 protocol.

That protocol was considered a breakthrough at the time, and was the result of a bilateral pact in March that year in which China agreed to protect U.S. copyrights and base its food safety standards of plant and animal imports on sound science.
In return, Washington agreed to support China's entry into the WTO.
Agriculture was brought under the aegis of the WTO at the conclusion of the Uruguay round of GATT, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade that preceeded the WTO.
U.S. officials have said they expect very strong agricultural trade reform proposals from China before it can enter the WTO.

Among issues outstanding is China's blanket ban on imports of wheat from the U.S. Pacific northwest on the grounds that it cannot be guaranteed free of a fungus known as TCK, which Washington claims in harmless.
